query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a trace amount of a reactive dopant into the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will promote the in‐situ formation of a stable, lubricious tribofilm during sliding, thereby lowering the coefficient of friction and wear rate across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Pristine CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix without the reactive dopant.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, low-volume fraction of a reactive dopant (without presupposing its specific chemical class) into the alloy during processing.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests performed under varying loads in an ambient atmosphere, with operating temperatures ranging from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Segregation of the reactive dopant to the sliding interface and its transformation (e.g., via controlled oxidation) into a lubricious tribofilm.
generation.mechanism: Under the applied mechanical stress and elevated temperature, the dopant migrates to the contact surface and reacts with ambient oxygen, forming a thin, stable oxide layer that acts as a solid lubricant. This layer reduces direct asperity contact, thus decreasing friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the doped alloy will exhibit consistently lower coefficients of friction and reduced wear rates across the full temperature span. The improvement is expected to be observable at multiple reference temperatures, including near room temperature and at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 704 °C and up to 800 °C).
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy without the dopant, which exhibits higher friction and wear, particularly with the challenge of maintaining performance over a wide temperature range.
generation.boundary: The expected improvement is bound to the tested temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C), under sliding conditions with similar loads and an oxidizing environment. Behavior outside these conditions (e.g., in non‐oxidizing atmospheres or at temperatures significantly above 800 °C) may differ.
generation.uncertainty: There is moderate uncertainty regarding the precise thermodynamic and kinetic behaviors of the dopant segregation and tribofilm formation, as well as the durability of the tribofilm under rapidly changing loads and environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy with the reactive dopant and one set without it (baseline). Test both using a standardized sliding tribometer with variable temperature control. Perform sliding tests at temperatures spanning from room temperature to 800 °C under identical load and environmental conditions. Monitor friction continuously and quantify wear via post-test surface profilometry and weight loss measurements.
measurements: Coefficient of friction at discrete temperature intervals (e.g., RT, 400 °C, 704 °C, 800 °C)
Wear rate (volume loss or weight loss) at each temperature
Surface characterization (e.g., SEM, XPS) of the wear track to verify the presence and nature of the tribofilm
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped alloy does not consistently exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the baseline alloy at the tested temperatures, or if no evidence of the predicted lubricious tribofilm is observed on the wear tracks, then the hypothesis is falsified.
